===  chart.py
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

data = {
    'Country': ['Morocco', 'Morocco', 'Morocco', 'Tunisia', 'Tunisia', 'Tunisia',
                'Egypt', 'Egypt', 'Egypt', 'Morocco', 'Morocco', 'Morocco',
                'Tunisia', 'Tunisia', 'Tunisia', 'Egypt', 'Egypt', 'Egypt',
                'Morocco', 'Morocco', 'Morocco', 'Tunisia', 'Tunisia', 'Tunisia',
                'Egypt', 'Egypt', 'Egypt', 'Algeria', 'Algeria', 'Algeria'],
    'Year': [2018, 2019, 2020, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2018, 2019, 2020,
             2018, 2019, 2020, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2018, 2019, 2020,
             2018, 2019, 2020, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2018, 2019, 2020,
             2018, 2019, 2020],
    'Sector': ['Manufacturing', 'Manufacturing', 'Manufacturing', 'Manufacturing', 'Manufacturing', 'Manufacturing',
               'Manufacturing', 'Manufacturing', 'Manufacturing', 'Agriculture', 'Agriculture', 'Agriculture',
               'Agriculture', 'Agriculture', 'Agriculture', 'Agriculture', 'Agriculture', 'Agriculture',
               'Mining', 'Mining', 'Mining', 'Mining', 'Mining', 'Mining',
               'Mining', 'Mining', 'Mining', 'Energy', 'Energy', 'Energy'],
    'Export_Value': [20.5, 22.1, 21.8, 18.3, 19.7, 18.9, 28.1, 29.5, 30.8,
                     15.2, 16.5, 17.3, 14.8, 15.6, 16.1, 22.0, 23.4, 24.7,
                     12.3, 13.0, 12.8, 14.2, 15.1, 13.7, 35.6, 37.2, 36.4,
                     42.1, 44.5, 43.2],
    'GDP_Growth': [3.1, 2.5, -6.3, 1.5, 1.0, -8.8, 5.3, 5.6, 3.6,
                   3.1, 2.5, -6.3, 1.5, 1.0, -8.8, 5.3, 5.6, 3.6,
                   3.1, 2.5, -6.3, 1.5, 1.0, -8.8, 5.3, 5.6, 3.6,
                   0.8, 0.7, 3.9]
}

df = pd.DataFrame(data)

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 7))
colors = {
    'Morocco': '#4e79a7',
    'Tunisia': '#f28e2b',
    'Egypt': '#e15759',
    'Algeria': '#76b7b2'
}

for country, group in df.groupby('Country'):
    plt.scatter(group['GDP_Growth'], group['Export_Value'],
                s=group['Export_Value']*20,
                color=colors[country],
                label=country,
                alpha=0.7,
                edgecolors='w',
                linewidth=0.5)

plt.title('North African Export Value vs GDP Growth (2018-2020)', fontsize=16, pad=20)
plt.xlabel('GDP Growth (%)', fontsize=12)
plt.ylabel('Export Value (% of GDP)', fontsize=12)
plt.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.6)
plt.legend(title='Country', bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 1), loc='upper left')
plt.tight_layout()

plt.savefig('output.png', dpi=300)

===  summary.txt
This scatter plot visualizes the relationship between export value (as a percentage of GDP) and GDP growth (in percentage) for four North African countries—Algeria, Egypt, Morocco, and Tunisia—over the period from 2018 to 2020. The chart employs a distinct color for each country: teal for Algeria, coral pink for Egypt, blue for Morocco, and orange for Tunisia. Each data point represents a specific year for a given country, with the size of the bubble corresponding to the magnitude of the export value, providing an additional visual dimension to the data.

The horizontal axis, labeled "GDP Growth (%)", ranges from approximately -9% to 6%, capturing periods of both economic contraction and expansion. The vertical axis, labeled "Export Value (% of GDP)", spans from 10% to 45%, reflecting the proportion of GDP attributed to exports. Algeria’s data points are clustered in the upper section of the chart, with export values ranging between 42.1% and 44.5% and GDP growth fluctuating between 0.7% and 3.9%. Egypt’s data points appear primarily in the middle to upper-right quadrant, showing export values between 22.0% and 37.2% and GDP growth between 3.6% and 5.6%. Morocco’s data points are more dispersed, with export values ranging from 12.3% to 22.1% and GDP growth from -6.3% to 3.1%. Tunisia’s data points are concentrated in the lower-left quadrant, indicating lower export values between 13.7% and 19.7% and GDP growth ranging from -8.8% to 1.5%.

The chart effectively highlights how export values and GDP growth rates have varied across these countries and years, with noticeable economic contractions in 2020 for some nations. The varying sizes of the bubbles further emphasize differences in export contributions to GDP, providing a clear and comparative visual representation of economic performance in the region.
